newsitem.title: UKRAINE: IMF visits Kiev as protesters take to streets.
newsitem.headline: IMF visits Kiev as protesters take to streets.

text.p: International Monetary Fund officials arrived in Ukraine on Tuesday to cast another critical eye on its bid for billions of dollars of credit, and economists said all was not lost despite this year's much-delayed budget.
A row between the president and a conservative-dominated parliament has served to prolong talks for months between the Fund and Kiev about a three-year, $2.5-$3 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF).

And with the last tranche of an $867 million stand-by credit paid out last month and a back-payments mountain exceeding 4.2 billion hryvnias ($2.3 billion), thousands of embittered communists took to the streets to protest unpaid wages on Tuesday.

Protesters were predicting the demise of the IMF credit and even President Leonid Kuchma's downfall on Tuesday as the head of the IMF's European II Department, John Odling-Smee, arrived for a three-day visit.
But economists said the wishes of the mostly elderly crowd, some of whom carried black wreaths emblazoned with the word "IMF", were unlikely to come true.
The credit has been held up by the slow passage of the budget and reforms through a parliament which is involved in a constant struggle with the government to ease up on reforms.
"It's no surprise the budget's being delayed. The fact it's always been tied to deregulatory reforms means it's proving rather difficult to get through parliament," one economist said.
"But there's still relative optimism that it will eventually be passed. Previous budgets have really just been a framework and there's never enough money anyway," he added.
Economists said Ukraine could comfortably get by without the EFF until the end of March because of cash from foreigners plugging in to the lucrative Treasury-bill market.
"There's been a lot of private money through T-bills. A few months ago it looked like they'd get past the end of March but now they'll make it past then comfortably," the economist said.
Despite such optimism, the government is clearly taking the protests very seriously.

The prime minister and other top officials went on a tour of industrial centres this month -- apparently enabling a decision by trade unions not to take part in Tuesday's "Day of Action" which was supposed to have been a nationwide strike.
Parliament's communist speaker Olexander Moroz blamed the government for not submitting a final budget document incorporating changes suggested by parliament last December.
"The budget will be passed two weeks after the government releases it to us, but until now we have received nothing from them," Moroz told a news conference.

The draft budget foresees Ukraine's first growth since independence in 1991, and initial versions called for a deficit of 5.5 percent of gross domestic product -- or four percent by Western calculations -- and annual inflation of 25 percent.

Economists also pointed to a cabinet reshuffle last month which saw off the ministers of economy, finance, statistics and machine-building as a sign that Kuchma himself was trying to shore up support.
The reshuffle was widely seen as an attempt by Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, whose impending downfall is being widely rumoured in local media, to save his own skin.

"The cabinet reshuffle is a response to the fact that whatever the government does, the economy declines further and they need more serious people. The people brought in have more credibility," the economist said.
But he added: "Predicting government changes is always a very iffy game but I think Lazarenko's days are numbered". = 1.831 Ukrainian Hryvnia)
